source: Greiner, Smith, Wilkerson (1989) A correction to the algorithm in Reiter's theory of diagnosis (AI 41:79-88), sections 1-3
finding: The bug is an interaction between two of Reiter's rules. The edge-pruning rule can delete a node n' that a closing rule relied on to close another node n. The path to a hitting set is then lost from both. It bites with non-minimal conflict sets.
numbers: Worked example: conflict collection {{a,b},{a},{b}}. If the root is not relabeled with the subset {b}, the 'b' branch is pruned too (since {a} is a subset of {a,b}) and the tree is left with one unlabeled root. Fig. 1 example: nodes n5, n7, n9 closed by the subset rule, then n' pruned.
quote: Reiter's description is incorrect in that some diagnoses can be missed under certain conditions.
limits: A published note with proof and examples, not an experiment. Reiter's text did discuss relabeling but the algorithm box did not state it.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 7 on what the bug is: prune plus close plus missing relabel on non-minimal conflicts. A model-written hitting-set routine should be tested on conflict families with supersets and repeats, against a vetted solver.

source: Greiner et al. (1989) section 4, revised algorithm HS-DAG and Theorem 4.1
finding: The fix builds a directed acyclic graph (HS-DAG) instead of a tree, so a repeated node is linked, not closed. The authors prove all minimal hitting sets are found and all non-minimal ones removed. The cost is that the structure is no longer a tree.
numbers: Three-part proof: (a) basic HS-DAG without pruning finds all minimal hitting sets, (b) pruning removes none of them, (c) pruning removes all non-minimal ones. Fig. 3 and 4: same example before and after pruning; node n3 keeps a parent so minimal set {a,b} survives.
limits: The resulting DAG depends on the order of the conflict collection.
agent_relevance: Gives an invariant a code check can assert: every minimal hitting set from a vetted solver must appear in the agent's routine output. The check is cheap and independent of the model.

source: Survey 'The minimal hitting set generation problem: algorithms and computation' (arXiv 1601.02939), seen as a search-result summary only
finding: The survey is said to describe the Greiner repair as trading the tree for a DAG, and to note HS-DAG can only be bounded by restricting depth. Not opened this session.
limits: Secondhand summary from the search engine.

source: Gap-search negative result: LLM-proposed conflicts inside a hitting-set loop (OpenAlex, arXiv API, Semantic Scholar, web search)
finding: No paper was found in which an LLM proposes conflict sets, code checks them, and a hitting-set solver finishes the job, compared with free-form listing. Web search returned the DX 2025 paper (Sztyber-Betley) as the closest. The arXiv API returned empty responses (rate limit or no hits), so absence is probable but not certain.
numbers: 0 matching papers in about 10 query variants. DX 2025 volume (OASIcs 136) lists 3 LLM papers: Sztyber-Betley (diagnostic concepts), controller auto-tuning, GEMMA-FD heat pumps. None is a conflict-checked pipeline.

agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. It is a clean experiment for us to run, not a result to cite.

source: DX 2025 proceedings listing, GEMMA-FD: zero-shot fault detection in heat pumps with multimodal language models (abstract)
finding: Zero-shot LLM fault detection from sensor series turned into text plus plots did much worse than a supervised model on the same prompts. This is detection, not diagnosis, but it is the other LLM fault paper at the MBD community venue that year.
numbers: Macro-F1 0.252 for GEMMA-FD (Gemma 3, open weights) vs 0.69 for XGBoost trained on the same prompts. One real heat-pump dataset.
limits: Abstract only read. Normal-vs-faulty detection, not component diagnosis. No larger or closed models.
agent_relevance: Agrees with the Sztyber-Betley picture that the model alone is weaker than the classic engine. Gap 2 (non-OpenAI frontier models, larger circuits) is still untested on real MBD objects.

source: Tie et al. (2025) CorrectBench: can LLMs correct themselves? (arXiv 2510.16062)
finding: Across commonsense, math, code and GPQA, intrinsic and external correction beat the baseline in most settings, but a plain chain-of-thought baseline is competitive on accuracy and efficiency. Reasoning models (DeepSeek-V3, R1, o3-mini) gain little from added correction and pay a time cost. External correction usually gives more gain than intrinsic. Mixing methods helps more but costs more.
numbers: 11 correction methods; models from LLaMA 3.1 70B to o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1. Table 5 first-column baselines include DeepSeek-R1 88.92 and o3-mini 81.24. The authors' explanation: reasoning models already contain internal reflection.
quote: Reasoning LLMs have limited optimization under additional self-correction methods and have high time costs.
limits: Per-method deltas not extracted. The explanation for reasoning-model results is a hypothesis, untested. Intrinsic methods here use extra prompts, so they are a different thing from a code check.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: for 2025 reasoning models a same-model review step has little left to give, and external checks give more. Spend the review budget on checks that the program can run.

source: Li (2026, posted Dec 2025) Decomposing LLM self-correction: the accuracy-correction paradox (arXiv 2601.00828)
finding: Stronger models fix fewer of their own errors. Detecting an error and fixing it are not linked. Telling the model where its error is made correction worse for all three models.
numbers: GSM8K-Complex, n=500 per model, 346 errors in all. DeepSeek 94% accuracy, 30 errors, intrinsic correction 16.7%. GPT-3.5 66.4%, 168 errors, detects 81.5%, corrects 26.8%. Claude 70.4%, 148 errors, detects 10.1%, corrects 29.1%. With a location hint: GPT-3.5 26.8% to 15.5%; Claude 29.1% to 12.8%.
limits: Preprint, single author, three models (GPT-3.5, one Claude, DeepSeek), math only, error types coded by the author. DeepSeek has only 30 errors, so 16.7% is 5 of 30.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the hard residue of a strong model's errors resists a same-model second pass. Also a caution that a location hint is not always help, unlike the true-location oracle in Tyen 2024.

source: Search summaries only: 'When does intrinsic self-correction help?' (2606.23196), single-utterance self-correction in R1 (2506.15894), dark side of intrinsic self-correction incl. o1 (2412.14959)
finding: Three more papers on self-correction in reasoning models exist. Their results were not retrieved. The 2412.14959 summary says failure cases appear even with o1.
limits: Do not cite for numbers. Targets for a later pass.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 is partly closed: two papers opened (d06, d07), three only listed.

source: Microsoft AI (2025) Sequential diagnosis with language models: SDBench and MAI-DxO (arXiv 2506.22405)
finding: A structured panel around the same model matches the bare model's accuracy at about 70% lower cost, and beats it when ensembled. Roles include explicit hypothesis tracking, a challenger who seeks disconfirming evidence, a test chooser and a cost steward. In manual case review the bare o3 anchored on its first impression and ordered 'reasonable' tests with no theory of information value.
numbers: 304 NEJM cases, interactive. Physicians 20% at $2,963 per case. GPT-4o 49.3% at $2,745. Bare o3 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO (o3) 79.9% at $2,397, or 85.5% at $7,184 with ensembling. Average +11 points on other providers' models. Single vs batched ablation (test set): both 83.9%, cost $3,991 vs $5,084. Example: bare o3 wrong at $3,431, panel right at $795.
quote: MAI-DxO often sought disconfirming evidence and switched its diagnostic path, while off-the-shelf o3 seemed to anchor on initial impressions.
limits: Authors are the vendor. No per-role ablation, so the source of the gain is not isolated. On the strongest reasoning models the gain was mostly cost, not accuracy. LLM judge. Physicians used a restricted interface.
agent_relevance: Nearest published test of gaps 3 and 5 on a real diagnosis task: structure (kept differential, forced disconfirmation, price per test) improves cost-efficiency. It does not show that the challenger role alone causes it.

source: Same paper, search of the full text for a role ablation (SDBench sections 4, 6, appendix)
finding: The authors write that for less capable models the explicit differential and test selection provide scaffolding, and for strong models they impose useful discipline. They hypothesise that post-training biases cause the bare model's behaviour. No per-role ablation was found in the text.
numbers: A search for 'ablat' found one hit, the single vs batched comparison only.
limits: Absence of a per-role ablation means the 'forced alternative explanation' effect rests on case review, not on a measured effect.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays partly open: a structural challenger step is used in a real system, but its isolated effect is unknown. We would have to run the ablation.

source: ACTMED (2025) Bayesian experimental design with LLM-simulated outcomes for test selection (arXiv 2510.18988, NeurIPS 2025)
finding: The LLM samples possible test outcomes and code scores each test by expected information gain (KL). This beat the LLM choosing tests itself ('implicit selection'), random choice and a fixed guideline subset under a three-test budget. Implicit LLM selection leaned on globally popular tests and did not adapt to the patient.
numbers: Datasets: chronic kidney disease, hepatitis C, diabetes. Models GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o. Five seeds. Budget of three features. CKD near-perfect for all methods (strong priors). KL stopping at threshold 0.6 cut the average to under two tests, about 50% fewer, with comparable or better accuracy. Per-cell accuracies are only in figures; not extracted.
quote: implicit selection methods showed a strong bias toward globally optimal features
limits: Tabular clinical data, not component fault models. Information gain comes from the LLM's own outcome probabilities, so it depends on the model's calibration. No exact accuracies read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a code-scored next-test choice beats a plain 'what next?' prompt in this one study. It is the same idea as GDE entropy probe selection, but the GDE form is untested.

source: Search summaries only: LDTL (arXiv 2604.05116) and CuriosiTree (ICML 2025) on active test selection
finding: Both build information-gain planning around an LLM for clinical test choice (greedy tree search weighing information against cost; a planner trained with information-gain supervision). Only the search summary was seen.
limits: Candidate sources for a later pass.
agent_relevance: Pointer only; not counted as evidence.

source: Gap-search negative result: LLM imitation of GDE entropy or minimum-cardinality probe selection, and LLM handling of superset diagnoses after a measurement
finding: No paper was found in which an LLM imitates de Kleer-Williams entropy probe selection or the minimum-cardinality split on circuit diagnosis, or in which new measurements adding superset diagnoses are tested. The nearest are d09 and d11, in medicine and tabular data.
numbers: 0 hits in about 8 query variants over web search, arXiv and OpenAlex.
limits: Absence of evidence; weak search tools.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partly closed (code-scored test choice works elsewhere); the MBD-specific question stays open.

source: Yaraghi et al. (2026, v6) Efficient black-box fault localization for system-level test code using LLMs (arXiv 2506.19045)
finding: An LLM can estimate which statements ran from a single failure log, without executing the code, and the pruned trace is close to the real one. Ranking faulty locations from the pruned trace is as accurate as the latest LLM-guided method with far less compute.
numbers: 785 faulty Python system-level test cases (industrial). Estimated-trace F1 about 90%. Block-level Hit@3 81%. Precision 82.1% at the best prompt; recall 95.7% at three functions. Pruning cut inference time by up to 34%. Against the latest LLM-guided FL method: over 85% less inference time and 93% fewer tokens.
limits: Localises faults in test scripts, not in the system under test. It starts from a real log of one failing run, so it is not model-simulated execution. Not an AutoSD replication.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 only indirectly: the estimate is anchored to a real log, and a cheap estimate of the rest is enough. Execution-grounded input beats full-context prompting on cost.

source: Beck et al. (2026) Towards a neural debugger for Python (Meta FAIR, arXiv 2603.09951)
finding: Models trained on execution traces can imitate a debugger (step, breakpoint, return) and predict the next program state. This shows that 'model-simulated execution' can be made reliable by training, not by prompting.
numbers: Next-state exact-match above 90% for step into, step over, step return and breakpoint (function level). CruxEval: small pretrained model (150B tokens) 53.6 input and 57.7 output pass@1. Fine-tuned CWM reaches 83.2% with the breakpoint action and 77.9% with step_return, +19.8 points over the stock model.
limits: Needs training. Python only, function-level benchmark. Not an agent study and no comparison with real debugger use in a repair loop. Repository-level accuracy is lower.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: prompted simulation lost to real execution in AutoSD-style work; trained simulators close part of that gap. Our scaffold cannot train, so call real execution where it exists.

limits: Search summary only. Earlier evidence (b20-b22) covers the original AutoSD numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open for current models.

source: Gap-search negative result: fault-model choice (weak vs strong fault) and LLMs
finding: No LLM study was found that varies the fault model or tests whether a model diagnosing a system with unknown failure modes behaves like a weak-fault engine. Sztyber-Betley and Plank 2026 remain the only LLM tests on real MBD objects.
